The aim of the following code is to broadly describe the data before diving into a more specific analysis.

### Loading libraries and the data

```{r}
#| message: false
library("tidyverse")
library("here")
library("patchwork")
library("gt")
```

```{r}
load(here("data", "03_cancer_augment.RData"))
```

#### Exploring the patients

From the data cleaning, we know that there are 1610 patients in this data set.

# Descriptive plots

## Cancer type and number of mutations

This plot shows the correlation between the different types of cancer, and the number of mutations that are present in the individual patients.

```{r}
ggplot(data = clinical_augment,
       mapping = aes(x = cancer_type,
                     y = total_mutations,
                     color = cancer_type)) +
  geom_jitter() +
    theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  ) +
  labs(title = "Cancer type and number of mutations", 
       subtitle = "The dots indicate how many mutations the individual patient has",
       x = "Cancer type",
       y = "Number of mutations") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

### Status and gender, colored by age group

Visualizing the LIVING and DECEASED patients based on gender and colored by age group.

```{r}
ggplot(data = clinical_augment,
       mapping = aes(x = status,
                     y = sex,
                     color = age_group))+
  scale_size_area(max_size = 20)+
  geom_count(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75),
             alpha = 0.8)+
  labs(size = "Count",
       x = "Patient status",
       y = "Gender") 
```

# Exploring the clinical data

```{r}
clinical_augment |> 
  group_by(sex, status) |> 
  count() |>
  group_by(sex) |> 
  mutate(percentage = (n/sum(n))*100)
```

The patients in this study are about two thirds men to one third women, with roughly a 50% survival rate, though survival of women is slightly lower than that of men on first inspection.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
p1 <- clinical_augment |> 
        ggplot(aes(x = sex,
                   fill = status))+
        geom_bar(alpha = 0.5)+
  labs(x= "",
       y = "Number of patients",
       fill = "Status",
       title = "Profiles of the patients in the cancer study")+
  theme_minimal()
p2 <- ggplot(data = clinical_augment,
       mapping = aes(x = status,
                     y = sex,
                     colour = age_group))+
  scale_size_area(max_size = 10)+
  geom_count(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75),
             alpha = 0.5)+
  labs(size = "Count",
       x = "Status",
       y = "",
       colour = "Age")+
  theme_minimal()

p1+p2+ plot_layout(widths = c(1, 5))
```

It is apparent that few patients are under 30 years old, with most in the 61-70 age group. This can also be seen via the bubbles on the right. Fewer female patients can be seen than males based on the bubble sizes, and the distribution of the age groups are also showing, that there are few patients in the \<30 age group, and most of the patients are found in the 61-70 age group.

```{r}
clinical_augment |> 
  group_by(cancer_type, sex) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = cancer_type,
             fill = sex))+
  geom_bar(alpha = 0.7)+
  theme_minimal()+
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(
    angle = 45,
    hjust = 1))+
  labs(x = "Cancer type",
       y = "Number of affected patients",
       fill = "Sex",
       title = "Number of patients affected by each type of cancer")
```

Eleven types of cancer are tracked in this data set, two of which (breast cancer and skin cancer, non-melanoma) affect only women or men respectively. Only one patient is affected by skin cancer, non-melanoma.

Below we have ordered the number of samples from each cancer type, disregarding gender.

```{r}
clinical_augment |>
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_infreq(cancer_type))) +
  geom_bar() +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 60,
                                   hjust = 1)) +
  labs(x = "Cancer type",
       y = "Number of samples",
       title = "Number of samples per cancer type")
```

We have now made a point plot showing the average survival for each cancer type, compared to age groups.

```{r}
#| message: false
clinical_augment |> 
  filter(status == "DECEASED") |> 
  group_by(age_group, cancer_type) |>
  summarise(average_survival_months = mean(os_months)) |> 
  arrange(average_survival_months) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = age_group,
             y = average_survival_months,
             colour = cancer_type))+
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7)+
  theme_minimal()+
  labs(x = "Age group",
       y = "Average survival (months)",
       colour = "Cancer type",
       title = "Average survival per cancer type")
```

Across age groups, melanoma and renal cell carcinoma are associated with higher survival than other cancer types, except for the \<30 age group, where renal cell carcinoma is associated with the shortest survival time. The majority of cancer types seem to have an average survival time between 5 and 15 months. Patients under 30 years old have the shortest average survival time, while the patients between 50 and 60 have the longest on average.

#### Exploring the types of mutations

Visualizing the number of mutations that affect each patient.

```{r}
ggplot(data = clinical_augment,
       mapping = aes(x = cancer_type,
                     y = total_mutations,
                     color = cancer_type)) +
  geom_jitter() +
    theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  ) +
  labs(title = "Cancer type and number of mutations", 
       subtitle = "The dots indicate how many mutations the individual patient has",
       x = "Cancer type",
       y = "Number of mutations") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

From this plot, we can see which cancer types have the most mutations, with each individual patient representing a dot in the plot. Types such as melanoma, colorectal cancer, bladder cancer and non-small cell lung cancer show a higher number of mutations than the others. Since renal cell carcinoma and melanoma was some of the were associated with the longer survival periods, there does not seem to be a correlation between a low number of mutations and a longer survival period, since types like melanoma shows a longer survival period, with a lot more mutations.

```{r}
clinical_mutation |> 
  filter(is_top_gene) |> 
  group_by(hugo_symbol) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = hugo_symbol,
             fill = cancer_type))+
  geom_bar(alpha = 0.5)+
  labs(title = "Number of mutations associated to top 20 genes",
       x = "Hugo symbol of affected gene",
       y = "Number of mutations",
       fill = "Cancer type")+
  theme_minimal()+
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(
    angle = 45,
    hjust = 1))
```

There are big variations in the number of genes with mutations. The TP53 gene is the most mutated gene in this data set and appears in all the cancer types.

```{r}
mutation_augment |> 
  group_by(hugo_symbol) |> 
  count(name = "nbr_occurences") |>
  ungroup() |> 
  summarise(mean = mean(nbr_occurences),
            max = max(nbr_occurences),
            min = min(nbr_occurences),
            median = median(nbr_occurences)) |> 
  gt()
```

This table summarizes the number of mutations affecting each gene. This shows the considerable variation in how genes are affected in all types of cancer.

## Location of mutations in the genome

```{r}
clinical_mutation |>
  arrange(chromosome) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = chromosome,
             fill = age_group))+
  geom_bar(alpha = 0.5)+
  theme_minimal()+
  labs(x = "Chromosome",
       y = "Number of mutations",
       fill = "Age group",
       title = "Location of mutations in chromosomes")
```

This graph shows the location of the mutations with respect to the chromosomes. The most affected chromosome is number 17, while the least affected is number 21. There are no mutations associated to the Y chromosome in this data set. Age does not seem to have much impact on the location of the mutation.
